title: Canada's largest banks move to keep personal AI agents out of online banking
excerpt: Several of Canada's biggest banks say third-party AI agents may not log in to customer accounts, citing security. What was decided, what is unclear, and what to ask.

sources.title: CP24 (The Canadian Press): Some Canadian banks blocking personal AI agents amid security concerns
Global News: Canadian banks and personal AI agents

body_html:
Several of Canada's largest banks have said that personal AI agents made by other companies may not log in to customer accounts on their behalf. Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) confirmed on 28 October 2026 that it blocks third-party personal AI agents from direct access to its logged-in digital services, including online banking, according to The Canadian Press. Other major banks described similar positions to reporters the same day.

A personal AI agent is software that can carry out tasks for you, such as signing in to a website, filling in forms or making a purchase, rather than only answering questions. To act inside a bank account, an agent usually needs the customer's password or a way around it.

What each bank said

According to Global News and The Canadian Press, the banks' positions as of 28 October were:

  • RBC blocks third-party personal AI agents from its authenticated (signed-in) digital services. Chief executive Dave McKay wrote that "nothing is more important than the security of client information," as quoted by The Canadian Press.
  • TD said it decided to block all third-party personal AI agents from direct access to banking information that requires a login, while it puts safeguards in place.
  • BMO said it does not allow AI agents to access its digital services or carry out transactions, and reminded customers never to share passwords, PINs or verification codes through an unauthorised channel, including an AI agent.
  • CIBC said it does not support personal AI agents opening or accessing accounts directly.
  • Scotiabank said it will limit third-party AI agents on its banking platforms while it monitors the issue.
  • National Bank said it is monitoring consumer AI agents and had not announced a block, according to The Canadian Press.

The Canadian Bankers Association, the industry group, told Global News it could not comment on members' operational decisions. The office of the federal minister responsible for AI told Global News that the government and banks are monitoring the issue, and said: "Canadians should be extremely cautious about sharing their banking passwords with anyone."

Why it matters for customers

The main concern in the reports is shared credentials. Global News noted that when a customer gives an agent their login details, a transaction the agent makes may not be treated as unauthorised, because the customer handed over access. In plain terms, the customer could carry the risk if something goes wrong.

What is still unknown

  • How the banks detect and block agents in practice, and whether a customer using one would be warned or locked out.
  • Whether any bank will later offer an approved, limited way for agents to act, for example read-only access or approval for each payment. TD's wording, "while it puts safeguards in place", suggests its position may change.
  • Whether Canada's financial regulators will issue guidance. None was cited in the reports.

Which Directives this touches

An agent that holds your password has, in effect, no limits. Directive 2, Bounded autonomy, says an AI should act only within limits you set, with your approval for important steps such as payments. Directive 6, Secure and supported, covers protecting access to the systems an agent touches. Directive 9, Accountable, asks that someone clearly answers for what the agent does. An agent that can be misused through a shared password is one nobody is really in charge of.

The banks' move does not say AI agents are unsafe in general. It shows that, today, there is no agreed way for an agent to prove it is limited, approved and answerable before it touches someone's money. That is the kind of gap independent standards are meant to close.

Questions to ask

Before letting any AI agent act for you, ask the maker: what exactly can it do without asking me, how do I stop it, where is the record of what it did, and who pays if it makes a mistake? More questions are on our Questions to ask and Security pages.
